blocks.heading: Key Concepts
blocks.html:
• Brain receives 15-20% of cardiac output despite being 2% of body weight
  • Two internal carotids + two vertebrals form Circle of Willis
  • Anterior circulation (carotids): frontal/parietal/temporal lobes
  • Posterior circulation (vertebrobasilar): brainstem, cerebellum, occipital
  • Neurons are exquisitely sensitive to ischemia — irreversible damage in 4-6 minutes
  • Blood-brain barrier protects CNS from toxins

blocks.heading: Normal Values
blocks.html:
• CBF normal: 50 mL/100g/min
  • Ischemia threshold: <20 mL/100g/min
  • Infarction threshold: <10 mL/100g/min
  • CPP = MAP - ICP (normal CPP 60-80 mmHg)

blocks.heading: What the Nurse Must Know
blocks.html:
• ACA stroke = leg weakness, executive dysfunction
  • MCA stroke = face/arm weakness, aphasia, hemineglect
  • PCA stroke = visual field defects
  • Brainstem stroke = crossed signs (cranial nerve + body), locked-in syndrome
  • Time is brain: 1.9 million neurons lost per minute of ischemia

blocks.heading: NORMAL FUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Uninterrupted cerebral blood flow
  • Normal neuronal metabolism and function
  • Intact blood-brain barrier
  • Normal speech, movement, cognition, sensation

blocks.heading: DYSFUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Ischemic stroke: thrombus/embolus occludes cerebral artery
  • Hemorrhagic stroke: vessel rupture (HTN, aneurysm, AVM)
  • Ischemic core: irreversible infarction
  • Ischemic penumbra: salvageable tissue — target for intervention

blocks.heading: ⚠ Risk Factors (Non-Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Age >55 (doubles every decade after 55)
  • Male gender (younger), female (older)
  • Family history of stroke
  • Prior stroke or TIA
  • Sickle cell disease

blocks.heading: 💡 Risk Factors (Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Hypertension (single most important modifiable risk)
  • Atrial fibrillation (5x stroke risk)
  • Smoking (doubles risk)
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Hyperlipidemia
  • Obesity, sedentary lifestyle, OCPs

blocks.heading: 🔥 Complications
blocks.html: Cerebral edema (herniation risk at 3-5 days) • Hemorrhagic transformation • Aspiration pneumonia • DVT/PE (immobility) • Seizures • Depression, cognitive impairment
NRG Opposite: Blood flow interrupted → neurons ischemic → neurological deficit → disability or death

1. Vessel occlusion (thrombus/embolus) or rupture (hemorrhage)

2. Cerebral blood flow decreases below ischemic threshold

3. Anaerobic metabolism → ATP depletion → ion pump failure

4. Calcium influx → excitotoxicity → cell death

5. Ischemic penumbra: viable tissue surrounds infarct core

6. Inflammatory response → cerebral edema (peaks 3-5 days)

blocks.heading: Key Detail
blocks.html: Ischemic stroke (87%): thrombotic (in-situ) or embolic (from heart/arteries). Hemorrhagic stroke (13%): intracerebral (HTN) or subarachnoid (aneurysm). The ischemic penumbra is tissue that is dysfunctional but viable — it can be salvaged with rapid reperfusion.

blocks.heading: Clinical Result
blocks.html: Ischemic core = irreversible infarction within minutes to hours. Penumbra can be salvaged for 4.5 hours with IV tPA (up to 24h with imaging selection for mechanical thrombectomy). Cerebral edema peaks at 3-5 days — watch for herniation signs (Cushing's triad: HTN, bradycardia, irregular respirations).
NRG Sequencing: Each step leads to the next — understand the cascade to predict S/S and management

blocks.heading: Early / Mild
blocks.html:
• Sudden onset: weakness/numbness (face, arm, leg — unilateral)
  • Sudden confusion, trouble speaking (aphasia)
  • Sudden vision changes (diplopia, hemianopia)
  • Sudden dizziness, loss of balance (ataxia)
  • Sudden severe headache (hemorrhagic)

blocks.heading: Severe
blocks.html:
• Complete hemiplegia
  • Expressive or receptive aphasia
  • Hemineglect (ignores one side of body/space)
  • Dysphagia, aspiration risk
  • Altered level of consciousness
  • Seizures

blocks.heading: Decreased LOC progressing to coma
blocks.html:
• Decreased LOC progressing to coma
  • Cushing's triad: HTN + bradycardia + irregular respirations
  • Dilated fixed pupil (uncal herniation)
  • Decorticate/decerebrate posturing
  • THIS IS A MEDICAL EMERGENCY

blocks.heading: Diagnostic / Assessment Findings
blocks.html:
• Non-contrast CT head: rules out hemorrhage (first test)
  • CTA/MRA: identifies occlusion location
  • MRI DWI: detects ischemia within minutes
  • EKG: identifies AF as embolic source
  • Labs: CBC, coags, glucose, troponin, lipids

blocks.heading: Link Patho to S/S
blocks.html:
MCA occlusion → Face/arm weakness, aphasia, hemineglect

ACA occlusion → Leg weakness, personality changes

Brainstem stroke → Crossed signs, dysphagia, vertigo

Hemorrhagic stroke → Sudden severe headache, vomiting, decreased LOC

blocks.heading: Cardiovascular
blocks.html:
• BP (may be elevated — DO NOT lower aggressively post-stroke)
  • HR, rhythm (check for AF)
  • Carotid bruits
  • Peripheral pulses, edema (DVT risk)

blocks.heading: Respiratory
blocks.html:
• Respiratory rate, pattern (Cheyne-Stokes = bilateral damage)
  • Airway protection (GCS <8 needs intubation)
  • SpO2, auscultation for aspiration

blocks.heading: Neurological
blocks.html:
• NIH Stroke Scale (standardized assessment)
  • Glasgow Coma Scale
  • FAST assessment: Face, Arm, Speech, Time
  • Pupil response, extraocular movements
  • Motor strength all extremities (0-5 scale)

blocks.heading: Key Laboratory & Diagnostic Tests
rows: First test — rules out hemorrhage in minutes

blocks.heading: Priority Actions
blocks.html: FAST assessment + last known well time. CT head IMMEDIATELY. If ischemic + within window: tPA or thrombectomy. NIHSS score. Airway protection if GCS <8. Nil per mouth until swallow assessment. Elevate HOB 30 degrees. Prevent complications: DVT prophylaxis, pressure injury prevention.

blocks.heading: 💊 Pharmacology - Nursing Monitoring
rows: 4.5-hour window; CI: recent surgery, active bleeding, INR >1.7
Give within 24-48h if no tPA; CI if hemorrhage
NOT for 2 weeks after large infarct — hemorrhagic transformation risk
Manage BP if >220/120 or for hemorrhage
DO NOT lower BP aggressively in acute ischemic stroke
Mannitol or hypertonic saline for cerebral edema

blocks.heading: tPA & BP Management Alert
blocks.html: tPA: 0.9 mg/kg IV (max 90 mg), 10% bolus, 90% over 60 min. Strict BP <185/110 before, <180/105 during. Watch for hemorrhagic transformation. NO anticoagulants or antiplatelets for 24h post-tPA. Do NOT lower BP in acute ischemic stroke unless >220/120 or hemorrhagic.

blocks.heading: Lifestyle & Patient Education
blocks.html:
• Smoking cessation
  • BP control (<130/80 target)
  • Diabetes management (HbA1c <7%)
  • Statin therapy (high-intensity)
  • Anticoagulation for AF (CHA2DS2-VASc)
🚨 Report Immediately: Decreased LOC | New/worsening neuro deficits | Severe headache | Seizures | Fever | Signs of aspiration

blocks.heading: Nursing Diagnosis
blocks.html: Impaired physical mobility related to neuromuscular impairment secondary to left-sided ischemic stroke as evidenced by right-sided hemiparesis, facial droop, and slurred speech (NIHSS 12)

blocks.heading: Goal / Outcome
blocks.html: Patient will maintain optimal mobility and prevent complications. Will demonstrate intact skin integrity and no aspiration events during hospitalization.

blocks.heading: Interventions
blocks.html:
• Position on weak side to encourage use of strong side
  • HOB 30 degrees, NPO until swallow screen passed
  • Passive and active ROM exercises
  • DVT prophylaxis (LMWH or SCDs)
  • Frequent repositioning (q2h)
  • Communication board for aphasia

blocks.heading: Rationale
blocks.html: Positioning on the weak side uses the strong side for protection and function. Swallow screening prevents aspiration pneumonia — leading cause of death post-stroke. ROM prevents contractures. DVT prophylaxis prevents fatal PE.

blocks.heading: Evaluation
blocks.html: No skin breakdown. Swallow screen passed — diet upgraded to mechanical soft. DVT prophylaxis in place. PT/OT/ST consulted. Patient communicating with board. Family educated on stroke recovery.
NRG Care Plan Formula: Problem → Goal → Interventions → Rationale → Evaluation

What system is being tested?

Neurological / Cardiovascular — cerebral perfusion and neuro protection

What is the priority?

Rapid assessment (FAST), CT head, determine tPA/thrombectomy eligibility

What is unsafe?

Delaying CT scan, lowering BP aggressively in ischemic stroke, giving food before swallow screen

What restores function?

Reperfusion (tPA/thrombectomy) saves penumbra; rehabilitation restores function

blocks.heading: 💡 Key Memory Aids for RENR
blocks.html:
• FAST: Face droop, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call — universal stroke recognition
  • tPA window: 4.5 hours from LAST KNOWN WELL — not symptom discovery
  • HOB 30 degrees: Reduces ICP and aspiration risk
  • NPO until swallow screen: Aspiration pneumonia is leading cause of death post-stroke
  • DO NOT lower BP: In acute ischemic stroke, elevated BP maintains perfusion — lowering worsens outcomes
NRG System Focus Formula: Stroke → Neurological → Cerebral ischemia → Neurological deficit → Priority: FAST assessment + CT head + Reperfusion if eligible

question.stem: A 72-year-old patient with a history of atrial fibrillation arrives at the emergency department 2 hours after sudden onset of left-sided weakness and difficulty speaking. The CT head shows no hemorrhage. The patient's BP is 178/96, and INR is 1.1. Which is the nurse's priority action?

options.html: Administer labetalol to lower the blood pressure to <140/90
Prepare the patient for intravenous alteplase administration
Begin oral warfarin therapy for stroke prevention
Insert an oropharyngeal airway to protect the airway

question.rationale: This is an acute ischemic stroke (sudden onset unilateral weakness, aphasia, no hemorrhage on CT) within the 4.5-hour tPA window. The INR of 1.1 is acceptable for tPA (must be <1.7). Priority is immediate tPA preparation — time is brain. Option A is wrong: lowering BP aggressively in acute ischemic stroke reduces cerebral perfusion and worsens outcomes. Option C: warfarin is for secondary prevention, not acute treatment, and is contraindicated within 2 weeks of large infarct. Option D: the patient is alert with difficulty speaking — an OPA is contraindicated in conscious patients.

why.html: Lowering BP in acute ischemic stroke reduces cerebral perfusion — only treat if >220/120
Warfarin is for secondary prevention, not acute stroke treatment
OPA is contraindicated in conscious patients; swallow screening is the priority
